extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners on formulating and supporting rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness), including when and how to rely on prior art, implicit disclosure, scientific theory, common knowledge/official notice, and legal precedent; includes examples of common rationales and when they do or do not establish a prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat any line of reasoning as a per se rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering obviousness, Office personnel are cautioned against treating any line of reasoning as a per se rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationales (e.g., automating a manual activity, making portable, making separable, reversing or duplicating parts, purifying an old product, “art recognized equivalent,” “structural similarity”) should not be applied as blanket rules. The examiner must explain and show how the rationale applies to the facts of the case at hand; simply stating the principle without an explanation is generally not sufficient to establish a prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale may be found in reference or reasoned from knowledge/principles/precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The rationale to modify or combine the prior art does not have to be expressly stated in the prior art; it may be expressly or impliedly contained in the reference or reasoned from common knowledge, established scientific principles, or legal precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite case law (In re Fine; In re Jones; In re Kotzab; In re Eli Lilly; In re Nilssen; Ex parte Clapp; Ex parte Levengood) for support. Examiner should identify and explain the source of the rationale and how it supports combining or modifying references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of some advantage is strongest rationale for combining references
rubrics_metrics.description: The strongest rationale for combining references is recognition that some advantage or expected beneficial result would have been produced by their combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantage can be expressly or implicitly recognized in the prior art or drawn from convincing scientific reasoning or legal precedent (In re Sernaker; Dystar v. C.H. Patrick). Examples of advantages: stronger, cheaper, cleaner, faster, lighter, smaller, more durable, or more efficient. A technology-independent improvement that makes a product/process more desirable can motivate a combination even without explicit suggestion in the references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal precedent can provide rationale only when facts are sufficiently similar
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may use rationale from prior legal decisions only if the facts in the precedent are sufficiently similar to the facts of the application under examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “Sufficiently similar” means the facts can be analogized to present the same legal issue; similarity need not be in the same technological area (KSR applied to vehicle pedal assembly). If the applicant has demonstrated the criticality of a specific limitation, it is not appropriate to rely solely on case law. Examiners must apply the law consistently and explain the analogy and applicability (In re Eli Lilly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale need not match applicant’s purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The reason or motivation to modify the reference need not be the same purpose or problem addressed by the applicant’s invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that the prior art suggest the combination to achieve the same advantage discovered by the applicant (In re Kahn; Cross Med. Prods. v. Medtronic; In re Lintner; In re Dillon). Courts have found a prima facie case when the art provided motivation to make the claimed compositions in the expectation that they would have similar properties even if for a different purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider implicit disclosure (inferences a skilled person would draw)
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering the disclosure of a reference, it is proper to take into account specific teachings and the inferences a person skilled in the art would reasonably be expected to draw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use controlling cases (In re Preda; In re Lamberti) to support drawing implicit teachings (e.g., implied substitutability or ranges). Examiners should explain why an inference is reasonable for a person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on scientific theory requires evidentiary support
rubrics_metrics.description: The rationale to support a rejection may rely on logic and sound scientific principle, but evidentiary support for the existence and meaning of the scientific theory must be provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Soli and In re Grose: when relying on a chemical/physical theory, the PTO must provide evidence supporting that theory. Where no accepted theory exists (e.g., crystal forms of zeolites), relying on a general chemical relationship may be insufficient to establish prima facie obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official notice / common knowledge should be used judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner may take official notice of facts not in the record or rely on common knowledge in the art only in limited, appropriate circumstances; such reliance should be judiciously applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer citing prior art rather than taking official notice. Official notice without documentary evidence is permissible only where the facts are “capable of such instant and unquestionable demonstration as to defy dispute” (In re Ahlert, In re Knapp Monarch). Examples: widely known basic facts (adjusting flame intensity). Do not use official notice as the principal evidence for a rejection; avoid when application is under final rejection or 37 CFR 1.113 action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not take official notice for disputed or esoteric technical facts without evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is inappropriate to take official notice where the facts asserted to be well-known are not beyond dispute or are not capable of instant and unquestionable demonstration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assertions of technical facts in esoteric fields or specific knowledge of prior art must be supported by citation to reference works recognized as standard in the field (In re Eynde; In re Grose). The Board cannot simply reach conclusions based on its own understanding without concrete evidence in the record (Zurko; Arendi v. Apple; In re Van Os).

rubrics_metrics.name: If official notice taken, technical reasoning must be explicit and clear
rubrics_metrics.description: When official notice is taken of a fact unsupported by documentary evidence, the technical line of reasoning underlying that decision must be clear and unmistakable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific factual findings predicated on sound technical and scientific reasoning (Soli; Chevenard). Present the basis explicitly so applicant can adequately traverse the rejection in the next reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: If applicant traverses official notice, examiner must produce documentary evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant adequately traverses a finding based on official notice or common knowledge, the examiner must support the finding with adequate documentary evidence in the next Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proper traversal requires the applicant to specifically point out the errors in the examiner’s action and explain why the noticed fact is not common knowledge. Mere request for evidence is insufficient (37 CFR 1.111(b); Chevenard). If relying on personal knowledge, examiner must supply affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.104(d)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of inadequate traversal by applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant does not traverse the examiner’s assertion of official notice or the traverse is inadequate, the examiner should treat the common knowledge statement as admitted prior art or explain why the traverse was inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If traverse inadequate, examiner should include explanation of inadequacy (Ahlert). This procedural handling must be clear in the next Office action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality considerations when adding references to support prior common-knowledge finding
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner adds a reference after applicant’s rebuttal only to provide documentary evidence for a prior common-knowledge finding and it does not create a new issue, the Office action may be made final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the newly cited reference introduces a new issue or a new ground of rejection not necessitated by applicant’s amendment, the rejection may not be made final. If no claim amendments, examiner must not rely on other teachings in the reference if making final (see MPEP § 706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Never rely solely on common knowledge as principal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is never appropriate to rely solely on common knowledge in the art without documentary evidence in the record as the principal evidence for a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board decisions require substantial evidence for findings; assessors must point to concrete record evidence supporting assertions of common knowledge (Zurko, Arendi). Official notice should be rare especially in final rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: When invoking legal precedent, explain and show applicability to facts
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner invoking legal precedent as supporting rationale must take care to ensure the rationale is explained and shown to apply to the facts at hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant has demonstrated criticality of a limitation, do not rely solely on case law. Examples of legal-rationale categories and how courts have applied them are provided to illustrate usage and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic design changes (ornamentation) generally not patentable distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters relating to ornamentation only which have no mechanical function cannot be relied upon to patentably distinguish the claimed invention from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Seid for the rule; exceptions may exist where shape/ornamentation results in a product distinct from reference (Ex parte Hilton). Examiners must analyze whether ornamentation affects function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of an element and its function is obvious if function is not desired
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of an element (and its function) is obvious where the function attributed to that element is not desired or required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ex parte Wu (omit polybasic acid salts when their function is unnecessary in certain environments); In re Larson; In re Kuhle. Examiner should assess whether the omitted element serves a function that would be desired in the claimed context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of element with retention of function indicates nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If an element is omitted but its function is retained by other claimed structure, that omission is an indicium of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Edge: elimination of a layer while retaining its function (erasable metal layer obscuring print) supported nonobviousness. Examiners should determine whether the function remains and whether prior art taught such retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automating a manual activity is not sufficient by itself to show patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly providing an automatic or mechanical means to replace a manual activity which accomplishes the same result is not sufficient to distinguish over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Venner: adding a timer/solenoid to automate release of a core was insufficient. Examiner must look for additional differences or unexpected results beyond mere automation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in size or proportion are not sufficient absent new results
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere scaling up or recitation of relative dimensions is not sufficient to patentably distinguish over prior art if the device would not perform differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Rose, In re Rinehart, Gardner v. TEC Syst.; if only difference is size and no different performance, claim not patentably distinct. Examiner should assess whether size change yields new/unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in shape/configuration are often obvious absent persuasive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The configuration or shape of a product is often a matter of choice and will be obvious absent persuasive evidence that the particular configuration is significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Dailey: configuration of a disposable container was a matter of choice. Examiner should require persuasive evidence that shape provides unexpected results or a new function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in sequence of adding ingredients are prima facie obvious absent unexpected results
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of any order of performing process steps or mixing ingredients is prima facie obvious in the absence of new or unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Ex parte Rubin; In re Burhans; In re Gibson. Examiner should determine whether reversing or changing sequence yields unexpected advantages or properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making devices portable/integral/separable/adjustable/continuous is not per se inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming a device as portable, integral, separable, adjustable, or continuous is not sufficient by itself to patentably distinguish over the prior art unless new or unexpected results arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Lindberg (portable not sufficient), In re Larson (making integral), and other examples. Examiner should evaluate whether these structural/functional modifications produce unexpected results or advantages beyond routine expedients.
